title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: demerit frees from cruelty charge, not motive of Jacob/Esau discrimination
pass_a_gloss: Further this also is to be noted, that we gladly acknowledge that in the reprobated subject there resides that contagion and unworthiness which can free the reprobating God not only from all cruelty and injustice, but even from the lightest suspicion of it. For to whomsoever this special mercy is denied, it is certain that he had no right to this, that such grace should be prepared or conferred upon him. But what is owed by no reason is reasonably denied, as Thomas rightly. To this is added that he not only has no right to such a benefit, but by his inborn vice is as it were proximately disposed to receive the vengeance of God. This Augustine explained most well, Against two Letters of the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 7. For the state of the whole human race represented to God electing and passing by is a state of sin, a state of death and of merited damnation. But since this state is common to all, and involves Jacob as much as Esau, it can be brought forward as a congruent reason why God can justly leave both, but it cannot conveniently be pretended as the moving cause why he rejected Esau, Jacob having been elected, who was in the same condition. And hence Dionysius the Carthusian affirms it to be intolerable that foresight of demerits be called the reason of reprobation.
pass_b_english: Note also: we gladly grant that in the reprobate subject there resides that contagion and unworthiness which can free the reprobating God not only from cruelty and injustice, but even from the lightest suspicion of them. Whoever is denied this special mercy had no right that such grace be prepared or conferred. What is owed by no reason is reasonably denied — so Thomas. Add that he not only has no right to such a benefit, but by inborn vice is as it were proximately disposed to receive God's vengeance (Augustine, Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7). The state of the whole human race as presented to God electing and passing by is a state of sin, death, and merited damnation. But since that state is common to all and wraps Jacob as much as Esau, it can stand as a congruent reason why God may justly leave both — not as the moving cause why he rejected Esau while electing Jacob, who stood in the same condition. Hence Dionysius the Carthusian calls it intolerable that foresight of demerits be named the reason of reprobation.
source_text: Porro et illud notandum est, nos libenter agnoscere, in subjecto reprobato residere illam contagionem et indignitatem quae possit Deum reprobantem non modo ab omni crudelitate et injustitia, sed vel a levissima ejus suspicione, liberare. Nam cuicunque negatur haec specialis misericordia, certum est, non habuisse illum jus ad hoc, quod gratia talis ei praeparetur aut conferatur. Rationabiliter autem negatur quod nulla ratione debetur, ut recte Thomas. Huc accedit, quod non modo nullum jus habet ad tale beneficium, sed est suo insito vitio quasi proxime dispositus ad vindictam Dei excipiendam. Hoc Augustinus optime explicavit, Contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2, cap. 7. Status enim totius generis humani Deo eligenti et praetereunti repraesentatus, est status peccati, status mortis et meritae damnationis. Verum cum hic status communis sit omnium, tamque Jacobum involvat quam Esavum, potest afferri ut ratio congrua cur Deus utrumque juste possit relinquere, sed non potest commode obtendi ut causa motiva cur Esavum rejecerit, electo Jacobo, qui in eadem fuit conditione. Atque hinc Dionysius Carthusianus intolerabile esse affirmat, ut praescientia demeritorum dicatur ratio reprobationis.
